8 . A reviewer has suggested that Thomson's argument for the permissibility of abortion
does not require that the fetus be a stranger. It is hardly obvious that the conscript would
have a duty to stay hooked up to an acquaintance, a friend or relative, or perhaps even her
own child. While I happen to think a parent would have a pro tanto duty to stay plugged in
to keep her child alive, it doesn't matter for my account. Even if parents do not have a duty
to bear burdens on a par with those of pregnancy to keep their born child alive, they clearly
have a far stronger duty to prevent injury to their own child than to an acquaintance; just as
clearly, the limits of that duty are debatable and context-dependent (see Section VI).

15 . Although she accepts Thomson's analogy, Flanigan does not draw on it in making her
argument. She shifts from an ailing violinist to an imperiled climber, kept from a fatal fall
only by a rope his climbing partner is holding ("Prenatal Injury," 35-38). She sees any effort
the partner makes to hold onto to the rope as supererogatory, so that while she has a moral
reason to hold on as long as she can (assuming some prospect of rescue), she would be
blameless if she let him go. But this is a more compelling case than Thomson's for claiming
minimal duties: the partner can't hold on forever! Because I think this example differs from
Thomson's in ways that strengthen the case for permissible withdrawal, I will stick with the
ailing violist in assessing Flanigan's claims.

Unlike Thomson, Howard does not assume that the fetus is a person
throughout pregnancy; he regards the early fetus as a nonperson whose "abortion is permis-
sible when the reasons for terminating the pregnancy, most often originating in maternal
autonomy, outweigh the relatively weak claims of the fetus." Ibid. at 248. If the duties of a
willing parent are unconditional even if the fetus is not a person, they will be, a fortiori,
if it is.

45 . Howard treats the prenatal responsibilities of intending parents as raising a straightfor-
ward All-or-Nothing problem. If the pregnant person genuinely wills parenting, she genuinely
wills the sacrifices involved in having a child. "However, if she is willing to make them, then
she cannot use the burdens of pregnancy as justification against the claims of the fetus."
Howard, "Maternal Autonomy," 252. If, however, an intending parent could change her
mind, she could revert to a mere carrier, for whom the second-best option would be permis-
sible, and sacrifices beyond those needed to give the child-to-be a life worth living would be
supererogatory.

58 . On an investment theory of parental rights like Millum's in Moral Foundations, the
two would seem to have similar claims to parent the child, since, as stipulated, they have
made the same investment in the child's well-being. I should stress, however, that only those

future parent. Someone otherwise lacking that right cannot acquire it simply by taking on
those duties.

70 . Ibid. We might explain the wrong committed by an intending parent in promissory
terms: a child could accept her parent's prenatal "promise" of a high standard of fetal care
and then hold them accountable for breaching it by prenatal neglect. Whether they could be
regarded as having prenatally breached that promise would depend on whether the child
would be regarded as having received a promise made to him at a time when he was incapa-
ble of uptake. Whether an intending mother could be seen as breaching a promise made
even before the fetus was conceived would depend in addition on whether a promise could
be made de dicto, then accepted de re.
